study_identification.title: Transdiagnostic dimensions of psychopathology explain individuals' unique deviations from normative neurodevelopment in brain structure

study_characteristics.study_objective: To test whether modeling cortical volume as deviations from normative neurodevelopment would improve prediction of transdiagnostic dimensions of psychopathology (p-factor model) compared to using raw cortical volume, and to investigate whether overall psychopathology explains overlapping abnormalities observed in case-control studies.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: ANTs; Brain extraction; N4 bias field correction; Atropos tissue segmentation; SyN diffeomorphic registration; Schaefer400 parcellation (400 cortical regions); Lausanne463 parcellation (sensitivity analysis); Custom adolescent template created from 140 PNC participants

quality_checking_detail.answer: Rigorous manual and automated quality assurance by three highly trained image analysts. Images visually inspected for artifacts and rated as 'unusable', 'decent', or 'superior'. Average ratings across three raters used as T1 QA metric. Signal-to-noise ratio (T1 SNR) also estimated. 47 individuals (out of original 1,601) excluded due to unusable imaging data; 83% of final sample had 'superior' quality images. T1 QA and T1 SNR used as covariates in some sensitivity analyses.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: All scanning performed on the same 3 Tesla Siemens Tim Trio scanner with the same 32-channel head coil at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania using identical sequences without hardware or firmware upgrades. Single-site study with no site effects to handle.

software_tool.answer: Not explicitly specified (custom implementation; code available at https://github.com/lindenmp/normative_neurodev_cs_t1)

response_variable.answer: Cortical volume (400 regions defined by Schaefer atlas)

predictor_effects.answer: Fixed effects for age and sex. GPR models age effects potentially nonlinearly.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study appropriately handles multiple sources of nuisance structure. Age and sex effects on psychopathology dimensions are controlled via nuisance regression (fitted on training data and applied to test data to prevent leakage). T1 QA and T1 SNR are tested and found not to significantly correlate with most brain regions (0.25% and 15.5% respectively), suggesting imaging quality confounds are minimal. Extensive sensitivity analyses control for additional nuisance covariates including years of maternal education, T1 QA, T1 SNR, and general intelligence (WRAT-4). The normative model itself accounts for normative variance and predictive uncertainty. Age is modeled using GPR which can capture nonlinear relationships. The study excludes 105 individuals with familial links to prevent correlation structure confounds.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Main text line 78-82: 'Within each fold, we applied principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of Z to the 9 PCs that explained ≥ 1% variance in the data. Additionally, age and sex were controlled by regressing their effect out of y before predicting y. Nuisance regression was fit on the training data and applied to the test data to prevent leakage.' Supplementary Methods: '105 more individuals were excluded because they shared a familial link with other individuals in the PNC (most commonly sibling relations).' Supplementary Results: 'In the normative sample we found that 15.5% of the Schaefer400 regions (62 regions) showed significant Pearson's correlations to IQ and 0.25% (1 region) showed significant Pearson's correlations to our rater-based estimate of scan quality, T1 QA, and T1 SNR.' Supplementary Figures S11-S15 demonstrate sensitivity analyses with additional nuisance covariates.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text line 78-82; Supplementary Methods section on Participants; Supplementary Results section on Normative models of cortical volume

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The normative model is validated using 10-fold cross-validation within the training subset (n=281 healthy controls). In this procedure, 90% of the training subset is used to re-train the GPR and generate z-score deviations in the remaining 10%. This yields validation on non-independent data within the same domain (same cohort, same scanner). Model diagnostics including out-of-sample prediction error and explained variance are reported for each brain region (Figure S5B), demonstrating that the normative models captured age effects well across regions.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Main text line 75-77: 'Next, we used 10-fold cross-validation to also generate deviations in the training subset. The 281 individuals in the training subset were split into 10 folds, wherein 90% of the subset were used to re-train the GPR in order to generate z-score deviations in the remaining 10%.' Supplementary Results: 'Figure S5B shows the out-of-sample prediction error and explained variance from the normative models run for each brain region. These diagnostics demonstrate that our normative models captured the effects of age well (as a function of sex) across brain regions.'
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text line 75-77; Supplementary Results section on Normative models of cortical volume; Supplementary Figure S5B

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The normative model trained on 281 healthy controls is applied to an independent testing subset (n=990) that includes 100 randomly sampled healthy individuals (from the original 381) plus 890 individuals with psychopathology. This represents independent validation within the same domain (PNC cohort, same scanner). The testing subset is completely independent from the training subset - no overlap between the 281 training individuals and the 990 testing individuals. Predictive performance metrics (RMSE, MAE, correlation between true and predicted y) are reported for this independent test set.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Main text line 68-72: 'In order to ensure that our analyses of deviations encompassed the full spectrum of psychopathology—including normal, subclinical, and clinical variance—we randomly sampled 100 of the 381 healthy individuals and combined them with the aforementioned 890 individuals to create a testing subset totaling 990 individuals. The remaining 281 healthy individuals were designated as our normative training subset.' Main text line 78-82 describes cross-validated prediction on this independent test set. Figure 1 and Supplementary Figures S9-S15 report predictive performance metrics on the independent test set.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main text line 68-72; Main text line 78-82; Figure 1; Supplementary Figures S9-S15

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not validate the normative model on data from a different domain. All data come from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC), acquired on the same scanner with identical sequences and no hardware/firmware upgrades. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the Discussion, stating 'this interpretation remains speculative, since our analysis was restricted to a single site. In order to examine whether the improved predictive performance observed here generalizes to new samples, future work should consider using a normative model trained on one site to understand variance in brain data acquired from a different site.'
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Main text line 59-61: 'All scanning was done using the same sequences on the same scanner without any hardware or firmware upgrades.' Main text Discussion section line 179-181: 'However, this interpretation remains speculative, since our analysis was restricted to a single site. In order to examine whether the improved predictive performance observed here generalizes to new samples, future work should consider using a normative model trained on one site to understand variance in brain data acquired from a different site.'
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main text Materials and Methods, Participants section line 59-61; Main text Discussion section line 179-181

clinical_dataset.answer: Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC) - clinical/psychopathology subset (n=990 in testing subset including 890 with psychopathology symptoms and 100 healthy controls; subsamples for case-control: depression n=136, ADHD n=163)

diseases_studied.answer: Overall psychopathology (p-factor); Anxious-misery; Externalizing disorders; Fear; Positive psychosis symptoms; Negative psychosis symptoms; Major Depressive Episode (MDE); Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

clinical_groups_n.answer: Overall psychopathology and dimensional measures applied to full testing subset (n=990). Specific diagnostic categories in full sample (n=1271): Psychosis spectrum:364; Major depressive episode:179; ADHD:206; Oppositional defiant:407; Social anxiety:295; PTSD:156; Conduct disorder:102; Agoraphobia:73; OCD:41; Anorexia:16; Manic episode:13; Panic:13; Bulimia:5. Case-control subsamples: Depression:136; ADHD:163

clinical_groups_age.answer: Testing subset overall: mean 15.13±3.54 years. Full sample: mean 15.10±3.64 years (range 8-22 years). Case-control subsamples: Depression: mean 17.57±2.3; ADHD: mean 13.62±3.11

clinical_groups_sex.answer: Testing subset: F 533 (53.84%), M 457 (46.16%). Full sample: F 668 (52.56%), M 603 (47.44%). Case-control subsamples: Depression: F 68%, M 32%; ADHD: F 37%, M 63%

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score quantifying deviation from normative neurodevelopment: z_ij = (y_ij - ŷ_ij) / sqrt(σ²_nj + σ²_ij), where y_ij is true cortical volume, ŷ_ij is predicted cortical volume, σ²_nj is normative variance, and σ²_ij is predictive uncertainty. Regional deviations averaged over ROIs for a priori regions (vmPFC/mOFC, inferior temporal, daCC, insular cortices). PCA applied to reduce 400-region deviations to 9 principal components for prediction models. Cohen's d for case-control comparisons.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Ridge regression (α=1) with 100 repeats of 10-fold cross-validation to predict psychopathology dimensions from deviations (9 PCs). Scoring metrics: RMSE, MAE, Pearson correlation between true and predicted y. Permutation testing (100,000 permutations) for significance. FDR correction (q=0.05) for multiple comparisons. Exact test of differences to compare deviations vs. raw volume. Pearson correlations between psychopathology dimensions and regional deviations with FDR correction. Bootstrapping (10,000 samples) to compare effect sizes (Pearson's Δr) between overall psychopathology and specific dimensions, with 99% CI. Case-control: spatial Pearson correlation between regional Cohen's d values for depression vs. ADHD, with and without controlling for overall psychopathology.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Modeling cortical volume as deviations from normative neurodevelopment significantly improved out-of-sample prediction of overall psychopathology, positive psychosis, and fear compared to raw cortical volume; overall psychopathology showed stronger correlations with deviations in vmPFC/mOFC, inferior temporal, and daCC than specific psychopathology dimensions; spatial overlap between depression and ADHD group-level deviations diminished when controlling for overall psychopathology.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Deviations from normative models yielded significantly better predictive performance than raw cortical volume for overall psychopathology (higher correlation r, lower RMSE), positive psychosis (higher r, lower RMSE, lower MAE), and fear (lower MAE). These three dimensions were the only ones predictable above chance levels in the primary analysis. Overall psychopathology correlated significantly with negative deviations in vmPFC/mOFC (r=-0.15), inferior temporal (r=-0.15), daCC (r=-0.12), and insular cortices (r=-0.11). Effect size comparisons showed that correlations between overall psychopathology and deviations were significantly larger than for specific dimensions in vmPFC/mOFC (vs. psychosis-negative and anxious-misery), inferior temporal (vs. psychosis-negative and externalizing), and daCC (vs. psychosis-negative and anxious-misery) at p<0.01. Mass univariate analysis revealed widespread negative deviations associated with overall psychopathology across cortex, including visual and somatomotor systems. Case-control analysis: spatial correlation between depression and ADHD regional Cohen's d was r=0.15 (p=0.002) without controlling for overall psychopathology, but decreased to r=0.08 (p=0.13, Δr=0.07) when controlling for overall psychopathology. Controlling for overall psychopathology shifted Cohen's d distributions significantly toward zero for both ADHD (t=9.65, p<0.001) and depression (t=24.42, p<0.001). Sensitivity analyses excluding n=142 individuals on psychoactive medication revealed additional significant predictions for psychosis-negative and externalizing from deviations. Sensitivity analyses controlling for maternal education and general intelligence reduced some effects below significance but deviations still outperformed raw volume.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Use of cross-sectional data to model neurodevelopment limits ability to characterize intra-individual variability; future longitudinal work needed to predict emergence of psychopathology over time. Focus on T1-weighted cortical features only; multimodal normative models may provide additional insights. Single-site study limits generalizability to different scanners/sites; future work should test normative models across sites. Controlling for socioeconomic status (maternal education) and general intelligence (WRAT-4) reduced predictive performance below significance for some dimensions, suggesting potential mediating effects of these variables on brain-psychopathology relationships. Sample restricted to ages 8-22 years; lifespan coverage needed to test developmental timing effects.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This study demonstrates proof of principle that recasting structural neuroimaging data as deviations from a normative cohort can improve predictive relationships between brain and symptom data. The combination of normative models and p-factor models may help separate disorder-general from disorder-specific biomarkers. Results suggest that abnormalities commonly reported in case-control literature (vmPFC/mOFC, daCC, inferior temporal cortices) may reflect general neural correlates of mental disorder rather than disorder-specific signatures. Visual and somatomotor system disruptions may be common across mental disorders and emerge early in disease progression. The study highlights limitations of case-control designs when overall psychopathology is not decoupled from specific dimensions. Authors emphasize need for dimensional approaches to psychopathology and brain pathophysiology to progress toward personalized medicine in psychiatry.

general_notes.general_notes: This study uses an extended p-factor model with 117 clinical symptom items (112 from GOASSESS interview plus 5 from SOPS/SIPS for negative psychosis symptoms) to derive 6 orthogonal psychopathology dimensions via confirmatory factor analysis: overall psychopathology (p-factor), anxious-misery, externalizing, fear, psychosis-positive, and psychosis-negative. Bifactor model statistics and factor loadings are provided in Supplementary Tables S1-S2. Psychopathology dimensions were transformed using inverse normal transformation to ensure normality. The normative model used Gaussian process regression (GPR) which provides not only nonlinear predictions but also regional estimates of normative variance and predictive uncertainty. The z-score formula incorporates both normative variance (σ²_nj) and predictive uncertainty (σ²_ij), distinguishing it from brain age models that typically use linear estimates and do not account for these factors. PCA was applied to reduce dimensionality to 9 PCs explaining ≥1% variance; PC1 from deviations was the primary predictive signal. Sensitivity analyses tested robustness across different nuisance covariates (age, sex, maternal education, T1 QA, T1 SNR, general intelligence), psychoactive medication exclusion, and parcellation schemes (Schaefer400 vs. Lausanne463). The study excluded 160 participants with gross radiological abnormalities or medical history impacting brain function, 48 for failing QA, 17 for missing demographics, and 105 for familial relationships, yielding final n=1,271 from original n=1,601. Unlike previous PNC studies, psychiatric history was not an exclusion criterion, yielding prevalence rates consistent with population norms. Code available at: https://github.com/lindenmp/normative_neurodev_cs_t1. Data available at: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/gap/cgi-bin/study.cgi?study_id=phs000607.v3.p2.
